Good morning, Excellencies, colleagues. I call to order the ninth meeting of the Economic and Social Council. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, I invite the Economic and Social Council to begin its consideration of sub-item A of agenda item 11, entitled Follow-up to the International Conference on Financing for Development, in order to hold the special meeting of the Council on Financial Integrity. Now, let me deliver my opening statement. UNGA riders, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, colleagues, ladies and gentlemen, It is my honor to welcome you to the Economic and Social Council's first ever special meeting on financial integrity. We convene today under a mandate entrusted to ECOSOC by Member States through the Sofia Commitment, which recognize that strengthening financial integrity is a systemic development priority that requires coherent multilateral action. Illicit financial flows continue to undermine domestic resource mobilization, weaken public trust, and erode the social contract, with the heaviest burdens borne by developing countries. Financial integrity is therefore not a niche issue. It is central to sustainable development, to fairness in the global economy, and central to the credibility of our institutions. At the same time, efforts to address the challenges span multiple policy and institutional domains. Standard norms and operational frameworks have been and continue to be developed across intergovernmental bodies. That includes tax cooperation forums, anti-money laundering and counter-financing of terrorism mechanisms, anti-corruption treaty bodies, customs cooperation organizations, financial regulatory standard-setters, and law enforcement networks. It plays an indispensable role in addressing illicit financial flows. Yet, gaps and asymmetries are inevitable. This is precisely where ECOSOC has a valuable role to play. The mandate we receive in Serbia is clear. We must foster a systemic high-level dialogue to enhance financial integrity. We must discuss the unintended consequences of related policies, and we must access best practices, including the use of technology to effectively combat illicit financial flows. As the President of the Council, I want to emphasize that ECOSOC is uniquely positioned to be the coordination space for this agenda. While specialized bodies platform perform essential technical work, the United Nations, under the auspices of the ECOSOC, provides the inclusive platform necessary to connect experiences, highlight gaps, and support more coherent implementations across processes. Today's meeting reflects that coordination role. Our first segment focuses on strengthening global coordination on policy and norm setting for the exchange of information and data, recognizing that transparency frameworks and data sharing arrangements must be fair, accessible, and governed in a way that supports all countries. Our second segment turns to be enforcement capacities and innovations, acknowledging that standards alone are insufficient if countries lack the tools to act on the information available to them to implement existing frameworks. Importantly, this special meeting complements but does not replace ongoing work in other intergovernmental and technical forums. I believe this is a historic opportunity. This is the first time that many of the intergovernmental and technical forums working on financial integrity have sat together. I truly appreciate the inclusive nature of the discussions to come. It is important that we share perspective and enhance coordination. Excellencies, in this regard, I would like to highlight the ongoing work of the subsidiary bodies of the Council. The Commission on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice is a functional commission of ECOSOC set off in 1992. The Commission acts is the principal policy-making body of the United Nations in the field of crime prevention and criminal justice, and also functions as a key governing body of the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime. The United Nations Committee of Experts on International Cooperation in Tax Matters has contributed practical tools to support countries, particularly developing countries, in strengthening tax transparency. This expert work is complemented by the Council's annual convening of an ECOSOC special meeting on international cooperation on tax matters, which provides a platform to address tax-related challenges, including those linked to illicit financial flows. The Council also oversees the Committee of Experts on Public Administration, which studies and makes recommendations to improve governance and public administration structure. Excellencies, the outcome of today's discussions, including the summary of the President, will help inform the ECOSOC Forum on Financing for Development, ongoing negotiation on the United Nations Framework Convention on International Tax Cooperation and processes under the United Nations Convention against Corruption, among others. In this way, ECOSOC contributes to strengthening coherence and supporting implementation across the financial integrity agenda. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, I encourage all delegations and stakeholders to engage actively and constructively in our discussion today. Your experiences, your perspectives, and your practical insights are essential to shaping more coherent, more inclusive, and more effective approaches. Let us use this space under the ECOSOC's auspices to strengthen coordination, to close gaps, and to ensure that our collective efforts on financial integrity better support sustainable development for all. I thank you. I now invite Mr. Guy Ryder, Under-Secretary-General for Policy, to deliver a statement on behalf of the Secretary-General.

I thank the Under-Secretary-General for Policy Guidance. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, unfortunately, Professor Joseph Stiglitz could not be here today. Thank you, Mr. President of the Economic and Social Council and Mr. Secretary General for Policy at the UN and member states and everyone here. So I'm going to read Professor Stiglitz's speech. As negotiations for a framework convention on international tax cooperation have resumed this week at the United Nations, we stand at a critical juncture in the global fight for financial integrity. The choices we make here about transparency, accountability, and the fair global taxation will shape not only the future of international cooperation, but the very capacity of governments to serve their people. This is a moment that demands both clarity about the failures that brought us here and courage to pursue the systemic reforms our world so urgently needs. Global finance is currently skewed as gaps, loopholes, and shortcomings in rules and their implementation allow tax abuses, corruption, and money laundering to flourish, and financial integrity has become one of the defining issues of our time, not because it is new, but because the costs of its absence have become impossible to ignore. When vast amounts of wealth can be hidden, shifted or stolen with impunity, we should not be surprised that trust in institutions erodes, inequality widens and democracy itself becomes under strain. We are living through a moment when, once again, we are reminded of an old truth: power tends to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely. In the Trump era, we say how disdain for trans-- we saw-- sorry. In the Trump era, we saw how disdain for transparency, the normalization of conflicts of interest, and the open encouragement for tax evasion and corruption at the top corrode governance from within. The recent OECD G20 agreement exempting US multinationals from the 15% minimum tax is a blunt example of this kind of coercive power in action. But this problem is far bigger than any one country or any one leader. The diagnosis is by now clear and well documented. Illicit financial flows, aggressive tax avoidance, money laundering, corruption and secrecy are not accidents or marginal abuses. They are the predictable systemic outcomes of a global financial system designed with loopholes, opacities, and asymmetries of power at its core. Weak financial integrity fuels extreme inequality by allowing those at the top to escape taxation, steal public resources, hide assets, and launder money, while ordinary citizens pay the price. It undermines climate action by depriving governments of the fiscal space needed for the green transition. It weakens sovereignty, as states lose control over their natural resources, their own tax bases, and policy choices. And it corrodes democracy, as economic power is translated into political power, often behind closed doors and behind public scrutiny. That is why the question before us is not whether we should act, but whether we can afford not to act now. The scale of today's crisis, economic, environmental, social, and geopolitical, leaves no room for complacency. Financial integrity is not a technical issue to be postponed for better times. It is a precondition for addressing the defining challenges of our age. We are discussing financial integrity at a moment when multilateralism itself is under attack. Around the world, there are forces seeking to divide us, to weaken international cooperation, and to replace collective problem solving with narrow national or private interests. Trump administration withdrew from the UN tax talks, although the rest of the world continues negotiation as we talk now. Yet the irony is obvious. The problems we face today are irreducibly global. Climate change does not respect borders. Financial crises do not stop at customs checkpoints. Illicit financial flows move precisely because borders are porous to capital, even when they are closed to people. This is why defending multilateralism is not an abstract exercise, but than a practical. This is why defending multilateralism is not an abstract exercise, rather than a practical necessity. Financial integrity and transparency cannot be achieved by any country acting alone, no matter how powerful. Unilateral action is important, but without cooperation and coordination, it will always be incomplete and vulnerable to circumvention. The race to the bottom in taxation, the competition to attract hidden wealth, and the tolerance of secrecy jurisdictions are collective action failures. They can only be resolved collectively. Cooperation on financial integrity is also essential because it enables better policy choices domestically. When countries coordinate on tax rules, exchange information, and agree on transparency standards, they expand, not restrict, their policy space. They make it possible to tax fairly, to regulate effectively, and to invest in public goods without fear of capital flight or retaliation. Financial integrity, in this sense, is not a constraint on sovereignty. It is a foundation for it. And yet, there is now a growing recognition of the weaponization of globalization and international rules to cater to the whims of the powerful. where the strongest can exempt himself when inconvenient rules are enforced asymmetrically and with varying rigor depending on the identity of the accused or the victim. Valid tools to enhance financial integrity get misused for nefarious purposes, as governments are able to impose financial sanctions, restrictions of access to banking institutions against ICC judges, use AML tools and laws to threaten and silence opposition, including statements that NGOs receiving foreign funding is a form of money laundering. Use of asset forfeiture laws, especially those related to drug crimes. to corruptly grab land and resources to benefit the individuals or grab power for running drug enforcement agencies. This calls for strengthening accountability for the perpetrators, but also the victims and enforcers. We are not starting from scratch. Over the past years, there has been a remarkable convergence of analysis on what is driving illicit financial flows and what must be done to address them. The UN Facti Panel made this unmistakably clear. Tax abuse, corruption, and financial secrecy are not isolated failures. They are systemic features of the global financial system. Likewise, the G20 Global Inequality Report, which I had the honor to chair, showed that weak financial transparency and fragmented tax cooperation are central mechanisms through which inequality is produced and sustained between and within countries. The problem is not a lack of solutions. It is a lack of resolve to implement them. First, transparency must become the rule rather than the exception. This means full and public disclosure of who owns what and where. Beneficial ownership registries covering companies, trusts, foundations and similar vehicles must be mandatory, verified and accessible. It means moving towards global asset registries that allow tax authorities to identify and track wealth across borders. It also means public country-by-country reporting by multinational corporations, so profits, taxes paid, and real economic activity can no longer be hidden behind accounting fictions. Progress has been made, particularly on automatic exchange of financial information, but asymmetries of access to the information still remain. Too much of the information is restricted and subject in the case of much law enforcement requests to goodwill to cooperate and share information, instead of compelled by rules and laws with accompanying accountability mechanisms. Second, international tax cooperation must be fundamentally strengthened. The current system allows profits to be divorced from real economic activity, enabling large corporations and wealthy individuals to opt out of the social contract. Both the FATCA panel and the G20 report underscore the need for coordinated approaches that ensure income is taxed where economic activities take place, and that minimum effective taxation standards apply in practice, not just on paper. Information exchange must be automatic, inclusive, and usable by all countries, not restricted to a privileged few. Third, Illicit financial flows must not be treated as an unfortunate byproduct of globalization. This requires common definitions, shared data, and coordinated enforcement against trade mispricing, tax evasion, money laundering, corruption, and capital flight. It also requires holding accountable the professional enablers, banks, law firms, accounting firms, whose business model too often depend on facilitating opacity. Without addressing these enabling structures, enforcement will always lag behind abuse. Taken together, these recommendations form a coherent agenda, one that restores fairness, strengthens sovereignty, and rebuilds trust in public institutions. None of this is technically beyond our reach. What is missing is not knowledge, but political courage. If we are serious about reducing inequality, financing climate action, and defending democracy, then implementing these reforms is not optional. It is indispensable. The capitulation at the OECD Inclusive Framework to exempt US multinationals from the global minimum tax has cost member countries billions in foregone public revenues. And in doing so, has removed any last doubt that the failures of multilateralism represent a grave threat to national tax sovereignty. And yet, it is still possible for all countries to benefit by standing together in a collective defence of national tax sovereignty. The African group's leadership at the UN has created the ongoing negotiations of the UN framework conventions on international tax cooperation, and it is past time for the countries of the North to commit to an ambitious global deal to strengthen every country's taxing rights. This negotiation represents a historic opportunity to rebalance global economic governance and to place financial integrity and transparency at the center of the international agenda. Many of the issues under discussion, beneficial ownership transparency, a global asset registry, country-by-country reporting, automatic exchange of information, go directly to the heart of illicit financial flows and tax abuse. It is not surprising that leadership on this agenda has come primarily from developing countries. They are, quite simply, the main losers under the current system. Their leadership has created a historic win-win opportunity. By standing together in collective defense of tax sovereignty, both North and South can benefit from stronger taxing rights, greater fiscal capacity, and a more equitable global system. Much of the rules that decide who has the right to tax multinationals' profits were designed by rich countries at a time when many developing countries were colonies. The double tax agreements ensure that source taxation is limited to the benefit of rich countries where multinationals' headquarters are located. For developing countries, illicit financial flows are not an abstract concept. They translate into underfunded schools, fragile health systems, unsustainable debt, and delayed climate action. The fact that ambition is strongest where the costs are highest should tell us something fundamental about the inequities embedded in today's global financial architecture. But ambition alone will not be enough. What matters is the language and the legal force of what is ultimately agreed. We cannot afford conventions that merely explore, encourage or consider action. Financial integrity will not be achieved through voluntary guidelines. or best effort commitments. What is needed are binding obligations, commitments that require states to act, to implement, and to be held accountable. If the convention and its protocols rise to that challenge, they can lay the groundwork for a genuine reform agenda, one that restores fairness to the international tax system, closes the channels of illicit financial flows, and rebuilds trust in global cooperation. If they fall short, we risk entrenching the very failures we claim to address. Compatibility with existing frameworks developed at the OECD cannot prevent meaningful reform from happening. This process should deliver tangible win-win benefits to both developed and developing countries, result in a fairer international tax system where the taxing rights are allocated between countries to reflect economic activities that take place there, from employment to sales to an exploitation of natural resources. The concept of value creation has been exploited by multinationals to cherry-pick where to cost certain activities, from IP management to global procurement, claiming that this is where value is created. The reality is that multinationals' profits are global in nature, and it's difficult, if not impossible, to attribute them to a specific country using the current transfer pricing rules. A fair allocation of taxing rights is one that recognizes that the profits of multinationals are a result of supply and demand factors, from employment to sales, and hence, the only fair solution is one that allocates the profits of multinationals between countries based on a formula that reflects these factors. We must abandon the fiction that multinationals are collections of independent entities. We need to transition to unitary taxation with formulaic apportionment, taxing corporations as single firms, and allocate their profits based on a just formula. This will require country-by-country information on the activities of multinationals to be available to all tax authorities. which could be achieved by the creation of a central public database for country-by-country reports, a commitment included in the outcome document of the Compromiso de Sevilla. The Framework Convention can and should enable this paradigmatic shift. At the same time, we must be clear, global cooperation does not absolve governments of responsibility at home. There is much that countries can do and must do unilaterally, even as international reforms advance. Governments can strengthen beneficial ownership registries, enforce existing tax laws, strengthen the work of anti-corruption bodies and anti-money laundering and financial intelligence units, regulate professional enablers of secrecy, and make country-by-country reporting for multinationals public. History shows us that transformative change often begins with political courage at the national level. Many of the policies we now regard as indispensable, from progressive taxation to financial regulation, were once dismissed as unrealistic or radical. They became possible because leaders were forced to recognize the scale of the challenge and the political pressure made them to act accordingly. Today is such a moment. The concentration of wealth and power we see today is not sustainable economically, socially, or politically. This message of ambition must run through everything we do. Financial integrity is not a narrow compliance agenda. It is about reclaiming the capacity of democratic states to govern in the public interest to deliver public services. The taxation of capital and the super-rich must work as a unifying strategy for mobilizing democratic forces. It is about ensuring that those who benefit most from globalization contribute their fair share. and it is about creating the fiscal and institutional foundations for a more equal, sustainable, and resilient world. We know what needs to be done. We know that the costs of inaction are enormous. The question is whether we will rise to the occasion. The stakes could not be higher, and neither could the responsibility we bear at this moment in history. Thank you very much.

Because I think the aim is that to make whatever mechanism we are working on workable for everyone, not for just one side and not the other. So there are key issues repeatedly raised in particular regarding two aspects. which is one is strengthening global coordination on policy and norm setting for exchange of information and data. One relates to how fairness is reflected in implementation of existing standards, particularly for developing countries. We are hearing that developing countries are investing significant time, resources, and administrative capacity in building infrastructure primarily to provide information externally. rather than being able to prioritize their own domestic policy needs. Very often, countries do not receive the information they request, as forcible relevance standard is subject to different interpretations and may, in practice, be used as a strategy to delay or limit information sharing. In other cases, the requested state set concerns about the taxpayers' rights to privacy, even though the requesting state has rules regarding the confidentiality of taxpayer information. One of the most significant concerns is the absence of an effective mechanism to report countries or jurisdictions that do not share information. Peer reviews are intended to serve this function, yet it's widely observed that jurisdictions that are reported often end up receiving surprisingly positive review outcomes. Complaints also criticize the limited use that can be made of the information exchanged, as it cannot be used for purposes beyond the specific tax-related matter for which it was requested without the approval of the country providing the information, approval that often is denied. The second complaint is related to how rules and the standards were made, including participation and voice. Several countries have stressed that they were not meaningfully part of the process through which certain standards were developed. As a result, those standards may not always be well suited to their specific circumstances. For instance, they are not adapted for highly informal economies. Furthermore, under the global forum, the standards to be implemented were developed before many of them were even in the room. Addressing these concerns is essential to strengthening trust, ownership, and the effectiveness of international cooperation on policy and norm setting for exchange of information and data on tax issues. Concerns have also been expressed about some assessments and surveys to evaluate the system that focus primarily on what developing countries lack, staffing, infrastructure, procedural knowledge, rather than reflecting shared responsibilities or systematic constraints, creating a sense that the burden of compliance challenges is viewed mainly as a developing country problem, rather than as an issue requiring balanced solution and mutual understanding. The concerns I have outlined now, ranging from imbalance in implementation to historical exclusion from standard settings, point us toward a clear and necessary path forward. We cannot simply continue to patch a system that many of our members Phil was built without them. The way forward must build on three fundamental pillars. First, we must move from consultation to true co-creation. It is no longer sufficient to ask developing countries to implement the standards developed in rooms where they were not present. Current standards and future ones must be designed by all to ensure they are adapt to diverse economic realities. Second, we need to restore reciprocity and trust. The exchange of information cannot be one way street where developing countries invest scarce resources to provide data, yet face procedural barriers like forcible relevance or privacy objections when they request it in return. We need a system with effective mechanisms that hold all jurisdictions accountable, ensuring that transparency is not just a burden for developing world, but a shared global obligation. Finally, we must reframe our approach to capacity. We must stop viewing the challenges solely as developing country problem, defined by what they lack in staffing or infrastructure. Instead, we must recognize the systemic constraints of the current architecture and build a framework that support our domestic policy rather than just our external reporting obligations. Mr. Chair, I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the Alliance of Small Island States. AOSIS strongly supports efforts to strengthen global coordination on policy and norm setting for the exchange of information and data. For SIDS, transparency is a practical necessity to protect limited fiscal space, safeguard financial integrity, and ensure that globalization works fairly for all. But we must also speak honestly about the unintended consequences of how global financial and transparency standards are currently designed and implemented. For many SIDS, these frameworks, while well-intended, have contributed not to inclusion, but to exclusion from the international financial system. Over the past decade, the cumulative effects of FAFT standards, AML/CFT requirements, and blacklisting by certain jurisdictions has resulted in widespread de-risking. For many SIDS, the consequences have been severe and immediate. The FAFT related risk perceptions have led to the withdrawal of correspondent banking relationships and payment channels restricted, even in cases where jurisdictions are assessed as largely compliant. According to the World Bank, over 75% of Caribbean banks experience a loss of correspondent banking relationships. Since 2011, the Pacific has seen a 60% drop in CBRs, double the world average. This is not technical inconvenience. Such structural bias against small markets rather than evidence-based risk directly undermines our trade, remittances, humanitarian transfers, and disaster response. We also see similar gaps and asymmetries persist in access to beneficial ownership information, financial account data, and exchange of information. Many SIDS lack real-time access to the very data they're required to collect and transmit. Financial account data often flows outward, but not back. And so a paradox emerges. SIDS are required to meet the highest of global standards, but are simultaneously denied full access to the financial system for failing to meet standards designed without their realities in mind. As such, our economies are frozen out on the margins of the international financial system, undermining development and trust in multilateralism. Therefore, AOSIS calls for recalibration of global coordination on data exchange and norm setting, where fairness and accessibility are explicit objectives. Thank you, Mr. President. The IMF welcomes and strongly supports this special meeting on financial integrity. The IMF's work in this area has spanned over two decades now, focusing on the financial aspects of crime, such as tax evasion, corruption, organized crime, and resulting illicit financial flows to make sure that crime does not pay. IFFs are a systemic and transnational threat, undermining economic stability and eroding the trust required for an effective global financial system. For the IMF, IFFs are macro critical, with direct implication for fiscal sustainability, financial stability, and the functioning of the international monetary system. Left unchecked, they will continue to drain public resources, deepen inequality, and undermine the prospects for long-term sustainable growth. Tax crimes are a major driver of IFFs, weakening domestic revenue mobilization and limiting countries' ability to finance development priorities. Abusive but non-criminal tax avoidance can have similarly harmful effects, particularly when exploited in a cross-border context. Large disparities in national legal definitions and fragmented international tax regimes facilitate illicit flows related to tax offenses. Such structural gaps are exploited by tax evaders and other criminals, especially where unilateral enforcement efforts tend to displace risk rather than eliminate it. IFFs linked to tax offenses rarely occur in isolation. They're often intertwined with other financial crimes such as money laundering and rely on similar concealment techniques, such as obscuring beneficial ownership and exploiting regulatory and transparency gaps across jurisdictions. This is where the anti-money laundering and tax agendas converge. Strong AML frameworks can enhance tax compliance by increasing transparency, supporting detection of non-compliance, boosting enforcement, and strengthening deterrence. Yet these energies remain underutilized in many countries. The IMF supports its members in leveraging AML tools to support tax crime investigation and strengthening the analysis of cross-border financial flows to identify suspicious inflows and outflows that may signal tax evasion or laundering of illicit proceeds. The IMF also provides tax policy design and tax administration assistance to help countries tackle tax avoidance, including in a cross-border context. With its global reach and expertise, the IMF is uniquely positioned to promote policy coordination, data transparency, and international collaboration needed to address this challenge. But nobody can do it alone.
